kp.d: Valerie Radwaner defines diversity broadly around historically underrepresented groups, expressly including racial, gender, ethnic and sexual-orientation diversity. She argues that varied backgrounds, perspectives and ideas strengthen both Paul, Weiss and the wider legal profession.
qs: We think about diversity in terms of historically underrepresented groups in the legal profession.
Our definition is all encompassing and certainly includes racial diversity, gender diversity, ethnic diversity, and sexual orientation diversity.

Our long and rich history of breaking down barriers has taught us that diversity of backgrounds and thought—whatever form they take—makes us a stronger firm and makes the legal profession a more interesting, open, and inclusive community as a whole.

kp.k: Success is measured through lawyers’ achievements
kp.d: Radwaner says the firm ultimately evaluates inclusion through lawyers’ achievements, including careers within Paul, Weiss and accomplishments after departure. This conception extends success beyond current firm demographic counts to the longer-term careers of diverse alumni.
qs: To that end, we ultimately define our success by our lawyers’ achievements.
For some, it’s defined by their careers here at Paul, Weiss.
For those who go on to pursue other endeavors, we believe that their time at the firm ingrained in them an understanding of the importance of diversity.
We are so proud of them and they remain part of Paul, Weiss whether we can actually count them in our firm demographics on any given day or not.

kp.k: The talent pipeline begins in high school
kp.d: Paul, Weiss’s stated strategy intervenes before university and law school by partnering with nonprofits and high schools in New York City and Washington, D.C. The programs expose underrepresented young people to lawyers, judges, private practice and public-interest careers, addressing limited awareness of professional opportunities.
qs: We think one of the differentiating factors for us is that we start really early in our diversity efforts.
We begin to look for diverse talent in high school.

Every year we partner with non-profits serving underrepresented groups and local high schools in New York City and Washington, D.C. so we can reach young people who may not know about professional opportunities in the legal industry.
We provide programming and early exposure so that young people have a better understanding of what lawyers do, what judges do, and what private practice and public interest jobs look like.

kp.d: Radwaner distinguishes short-term recruitment, medium-term development and retention, and long-term partnership outcomes. The firm monitors utilization, retention, work assignments and promotion, using these data to examine whether diverse and female lawyers progress and why they leave.
qs: We have short-term, medium-term, and long-term goals for our diversity and inclusion strategy, and we continuously monitor and adapt what we’re doing.
But, going back to your question, a short-term metric that we focus on is, ‘How do we get these individuals in the door?’
The medium-term metric is, ‘How are they doing when they’re here?’
We constantly look at all the data that we have internally, including utilization and retention rates, work assignments metrics and promotion rates.
And long term, we’re looking at the diversity of our partnership, which is an all-equity, one-tier partnership, and the rates of promotion.

kp.k: Early relationships shape associate retention and development
kp.d: Based on the firm’s exit interviews, Radwaner reports that lawyers of color sometimes had difficulty forming important relationships with senior lawyers and clients during their first years. Paul, Weiss responded with voluntary formal mentoring for associates of color during their first three years, supplemented by monitoring access to high-profile assignments, client relationships and visibility opportunities.
qs: To give an example, we know that the first few years of an associate’s life are critical as it is a period when they are forming bonds with the firm’s more-senior lawyers and clients.
We also found through our extensive exit interviewing that lawyers of color were at times experiencing difficulty forming these key connections.
To help combat this, we developed a formal, voluntary mentoring program.
Each participating associate of color is assigned a mentor during his or her first three years at the firm.

We help provide the fundamentals for creating these relationships, and help nurture them, whether through monitoring career-enhancing opportunities such as high profile assignments, client relationships or other opportunities for visibility.

kp.k: Reported retention rates approach firmwide rates
kp.d: Radwaner attributes the firm’s results to mentoring and other development efforts, reporting that retention among associates of color tracks or is close to retention among all associates. The document provides no underlying counts, comparison period or methodology beyond the reference to internal data and exit interviewing.
qs: As a result of these and other efforts, our retention rates of associates of color track or are close to those of all our associates.

kp.d: Radwaner reports Paul, Weiss’s U.S. partnership composition at the time of the 2017 interview: women were 22 percent of partners, women of color were 25 percent of women partners, and 13 percent of partners self-identified as ethnically or racially diverse. She characterizes promotion rates for women and lawyers of color as strong but supplies no comparative rates.
qs: We have really terrific rates of promotion for both women and lawyers of color.
In the U.S., women are 22 percent of our partners, women of color represent 25 percent of our women partners, and 13 percent of our partners self-identify as ethnically or racially diverse.

kp.k: Recruitment and retention present distinct obstacles
kp.d: Radwaner separates a “Day One” pipeline problem from a “Day Two” retention problem. She says the initial pool of diverse talent is small and highly sought after, while firms must subsequently invest substantial attention and resources in development and promotion amid numerous alternative career opportunities.
qs: The biggest “Day One” challenge law firms face is that the pool of diverse talent remains small and many compelling opportunities exist for these highly sought after individuals.
So one key obstacle is the small population from the start.
“Day Two” is retention—once they walk in the door, how does a firm like Paul, Weiss retain this talent?
We spend a significant amount of time, attention and resources retaining, developing and promoting our diverse and female lawyers.
Our success rate is quite good, but many leave to pursue other opportunities.

kp.k: Market structures can impede partnership diversity
kp.d: Radwaner argues that slower growth in large-firm legal services after the financial crisis constrained partnership expansion, while mergers and lateral mobility also affected diversity. She reports fewer women and diverse lawyers moving laterally and says their underrepresentation in lateral hiring negatively affected many firms’ partnership diversity, while noting that she did not consider Paul, Weiss affected in the same way.
qs: Another obstacle relates to the overall slowdown in the market for large-firm legal services since the financial crisis.
However, many firms’ partnership ranks are not growing at the rates that they used to, contributing to the difficulty in moving the dial in partnership diversity.
The industry is also seeing an increase in the number of law firm mergers and lateral movements.
With respect to the lateral market specifically, you see fewer women and fewer diverse lawyers moving laterally.
And that has had a negative impact on the diversity of many firms’ partnerships.

kp.k: Non-equity tracks may concentrate underrepresented lawyers
kp.d: Radwaner observes that many firms had introduced non-equity partnership tracks and asserts that women and diverse lawyers were represented in those ranks disproportionately. The source does not provide numerical evidence or specify whether this observation rests on Paul, Weiss data or broader industry data.
qs: We’ve also seen many firms create a non-equity track.
I don’t think it would surprise anyone to know that women and diverse lawyers are in these ranks in a disproportionate manner.

kp.k: Competitive pressures can weaken inclusion commitments
kp.d: Radwaner says some large firms respond to intense competition by deprioritizing inclusive culture. Her position is that business performance and diversity are aligned, rather than competing objectives, and that a diverse and inclusive workforce supports the quality and success of legal work and the firm’s business.
qs: Finally, the highly competitive market in big law has led some firms to put fostering a culture of inclusion on the back burner.
Some firms don’t recognize that business and diversity are in fact aligned.
We, however, appreciate that building a diverse and inclusive workforce is not only the right thing to do, it also ensures success in all aspects of our work and our business.

kp.k: Clients can drive diversity through accountability
kp.d: Radwaner reports that clients scrutinize diversity during initial meetings, ongoing relationships and requests for proposals. Requests for team diversity, demographic disclosures and periodic updates create provider-side accountability; she argues that greater client demands for accountability can foster broader change.
qs: We have seen regular scrutiny and a heightened level of awareness, discussion and focus from clients when it comes to diversity and inclusion.
It’s an important part of the discussion at the initial meeting with a client as well as in our ongoing client relationships.
When a client says that they want to see a diverse team, we listen – and we respond.
There may be an RFP where we have to provide diversity demographics and address some key questions regarding our diversity and inclusion efforts and strategy.
When we are hired, it is not unusual for clients to request periodic updating of our diversity information.
The more accountability we’re asked to provide, the more change clients can help foster.

kp.k: Law firms also advise clients on diversity
kp.d: The relationship is described as bidirectional: beyond responding to client scrutiny, Paul, Weiss advises private-equity and hedge-fund clients examining their own diversity strategies and infrastructure. Radwaner presents diversity initiatives and best-practice guidance as part of the trusted-adviser relationship.
qs: We are also now helping clients.
One thing that I have found particularly interesting in working with private equity and hedge funds is that many of them are closely examining their diversity strategies and infrastructures.
As trusted advisors, many have turned to us for guidance, best practices, and information on diversity initiatives, programs and strategies.
We have partnered with many clients in these endeavors in several different ways.

kp.k: Communication and transparency are central recommendations
kp.d: Radwaner recommends firmwide discussion supported by leadership, participation across career levels, interfirm sharing of effective and ineffective practices, and continued client pressure for transparency and accountability. She argues that closed-door deliberation by a small group failed to resolve diversity problems.
qs: Communication and transparency.
For a long time, this conversation happened at law firms behind closed doors with a small group of people wondering what we were going to do to fix these issues.
That didn’t work.
Within a firm, these discussions need to occur across all levels, with a focused level of commitment from firm leadership.
We also need more transparency across the legal industry.
Law firms are competitive, but frankly sharing best practices on what has worked and what hasn’t worked when it comes to diversity and inclusion is vital.
They need to continue to push us for greater transparency and accountability about the firm’s values, beliefs and commitment to diversity and inclusion.

kp.k: The source makes no claims about AI
kp.d: The substantive interview concerns diversity and inclusion in corporate law firms, including recruitment, work allocation, mentoring, retention, partnership structure and client influence. It does not discuss artificial intelligence, automation, legal technology, AI-related task change, pricing, professional regulation or access to justice.
